cards.title: A barrier to NP-hardness proofs for non-disjoint Kolmogorov promise problems
cards.formal: Is there a mathematically specified barrier explaining the difficulty of proving NP-hardness of Gap(K^SAT versus K), the source’s potentially non-disjoint promise-problem family? For an approximation polynomial τ, its yes instances are (x,1ˢ,1ᵗ) with K^{t,SAT}(x)≤s, and its no instances are those with K^{τ(|x|,t)}(x)>s+log₂τ(|x|,t). The yes side allows a SAT oracle and the no side does not. A barrier must concern this pair of sets, including its possible overlap. The source does not prescribe an obstruction theorem or a class of methods to which it should apply, so the requested barrier is not yet a complete yes/no proposition.
cards.why: Could identify which obstacles to reductions survive when a metacomplexity target is allowed to have overlapping yes and no sets, clarifying the scope of connections between worst-case hardness, average-case hardness and pseudorandomness.

sentences: The target compares short SAT-oracle descriptions of a string with longer descriptions that have no oracle.
Its yes and no sets may overlap, so a conventional separator may not exist even though mapping reductions can be defined.
The source asks for a formal barrier to proving NP-hardness of this target.
A standard barrier statement for a disjoint minimization problem would imply an unconditional complexity separation if transplanted here.
The source still does not fix the obstruction, reduction class or approximation quantifiers needed for one complete benchmark.

cards.definitions: Fix an efficient universal oracle Turing machine U. For a finite binary string x, a positive integer t and an oracle A⊆{0,1}*, define K^{t,A}(x)=min{|d|: U^A on binary program d outputs exactly x within t steps}, with minimum +∞ if there is no such program. K^t means the same machine without an oracle. SAT is the language of satisfiable Boolean formulas in a fixed standard binary encoding. The program length and runtime are different resources; t is supplied in unary, as is the nonnegative length threshold s. The input length is Θ(|x|+s+t) in a standard tuple encoding. The approximation parameter τ:N×N→N is a fixed positive integer-valued polynomial; τ(|x|,t) sets both the no-side time bound and the logarithmic gap. The source writes Gap(K^A versus K)∈P when some such polynomial τ admits a polynomial-time separator. A separator must accept every yes instance and reject every no instance; the requirements are contradictory on an overlap, which is not discarded as an ordinary off-promise input. Under deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions, SAT reduces to the pair when a total map R sends satisfiable formulas into the yes set and unsatisfiable formulas into the no set. This mapping condition can hold even if the target has no separator. The source’s surrounding discussion also considers weaker and randomized hardness notions, so the reduction class and the quantification over τ must be part of a proposed precise barrier. EXP is deterministic time 2^{n^{O(1)}}; ZPP is zero-error randomized expected polynomial time.
cards.answer_criterion: First specify the formal statement meant by a barrier, including its method or reduction class, assumptions and approximation-polynomial quantifiers. A complete answer then proves that precise obstruction or refutes the corresponding universal obstruction claim. The general request for some explanation has no fixed negation or acceptance criterion as currently phrased. A barrier for the ordinary disjoint GapMINKT problem does not automatically answer this question.

context_blocks.title: Non-disjoint is a deliberate feature
context_blocks.text: The paper studies pairs of yes and no sets that are conjectured to overlap. If they do, no separator can meet both requirements, but ordinary mapping conditions for a many-one reduction can still hold. Treating overlap as irrelevant off-promise behavior would change the problem.

context_blocks.title: The familiar non-hardness consequence behaves differently
context_blocks.text: For the disjoint GapMINKT problem, the source discusses the consequence that deterministic many-one NP-hardness would imply EXP≠ZPP. Proposition 1.8 shows that proving the analogous implication for Gap(K^SAT versus K) would itself prove EXP≠ZPP unconditionally. Thus the same statement cannot simply be imported as comparable evidence against establishing NP-hardness here.

context_blocks.title: Why this metacomplexity question matters
context_blocks.text: The source relates hardness of these oracle/non-oracle compression problems to worst-case versus average-case complexity and to pseudorandomness. Its 2023 version records further converse results concerning the family with oracles throughout the polynomial hierarchy, while retaining the barrier question. Those implications are progress on the surrounding theory, not a specified obstruction theorem answering this request.

cards.context:
The paper studies pairs of yes and no sets that are conjectured to overlap. If they do, no separator can meet both requirements, but ordinary mapping conditions for a many-one reduction can still hold. Treating overlap as irrelevant off-promise behavior would change the problem.

For the disjoint GapMINKT problem, the source discusses the consequence that deterministic many-one NP-hardness would imply EXP≠ZPP. Proposition 1.8 shows that proving the analogous implication for Gap(K^SAT versus K) would itself prove EXP≠ZPP unconditionally. Thus the same statement cannot simply be imported as comparable evidence against establishing NP-hardness here.

The source relates hardness of these oracle/non-oracle compression problems to worst-case versus average-case complexity and to pseudorandomness. Its 2023 version records further converse results concerning the family with oracles throughout the polynomial hierarchy, while retaining the barrier question. Those implications are progress on the surrounding theory, not a specified obstruction theorem answering this request.

methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. We aim for benchmarks of 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. All three use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The possible 1,000-problem expansion has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Deleted records are absent from the catalogue and exports. Their stable IDs and reasons are retained to prevent reimport. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The targets are 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. Top 100, Top 500 and the possible Top 1000 use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Records marked resolved are placed after the remaining candidates, without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.
